US Tariff on Swedish Tourism Services Hits Sector Revenues and Employment

A newly-imposed US tariff on Swedish tourism services has begun to affect the Swedish tourism industry, with firms reporting sharp declines in bookings and mounting concerns over job security. The 20% tariff, enacted last month in response to a bilateral trade dispute, applies to packaged travel products and guided tour services originating from Sweden and sold to US residents.

Industry representatives say the measure is already dampening demand from one of Sweden’s most important tourism markets. According to the Swedish Tourism Federation, US visitors accounted for 14% of international tourism revenue in 2023, spending nearly SEK 5 billion on tours, experiences, and cultural excursions.

“Our bookings from the US have dropped by almost a third since the tariff was announced,” said Karin Sjögren, CEO of NordScapes Travel. “We’re seeing immediate cancellations, especially for summer packages that are now significantly more expensive for American customers.”

Tour operators, excursion companies, and heritage site managers report similar trends, with many adjusting their forecasts downward for the remainder of the year. “The uncertainty is making it difficult to plan,” said Lars Hellberg, who manages Baltic Heritage Tours, which operates guided trips in Stockholm and along the archipelago. “We have already reduced our seasonal hiring by 20% compared to last year.”

The Swedish Association of Tourism Enterprises estimates that at least 1,200 seasonal jobs could be at risk if the tariff remains in place through the peak travel season. “Many of our member firms are small and rely on international guests,” said Association Chairperson Maria Lindholm. “The loss of US business is having a real and immediate impact on employment at sites, museums, and tour companies across the country.”

Analysts warn that prolonged restrictions could undermine the industry’s recovery from the pandemic. “The US has traditionally been a high-value market for Sweden’s tourism sector,” said Erik Dahl, a tourism economist at the University of Gothenburg. “Extended barriers risk eroding market share and weakening the financial position of many firms.”

Negotiations between Swedish and US officials are ongoing, but industry leaders are urging policymakers to prioritize a resolution. For now, uncertainty continues to cloud the outlook for Swedish tourism firms, workers, and sites dependent on American visitors.
